title: Best Websites to Find For Sale By Owner Homes (Investor's Guide)
excerpt: FSBO listings are goldmines for real estate investors who know where to look. This guide breaks down the best websites to find for sale by owner homes and how to turn those leads into profitable deals.

sections.content: For sale by owner (FSBO) properties are one of the most underrated lead sources in real estate investing. These are sellers who have chosen to skip the agent, which often means they're more open to flexible terms, creative financing, and faster closings — exactly what investors need. The challenge is knowing where to find them. If you're building a consistent deal pipeline, FSBO websites should be part of your strategy alongside other motivated seller channels covered in our [How to Find Motivated Sellers: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers).

FSBO sellers are motivated by definition. They've already decided to act without hiring a listing agent, which saves them 2–3% in commission. That savings mindset makes many of them receptive to investor offers — especially if the property needs work or they need to sell quickly. According to the National Association of Realtors, roughly 7% of home sales each year are FSBOs, and in investor-friendly markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), those numbers can represent hundreds of deals annually.
The Best Websites to Find For Sale By Owner Homes
1. Zillow — The Biggest Pool of FSBO Listings

Zillow is the most trafficked real estate site in the United States, and it has a dedicated FSBO section that's surprisingly robust. Sellers can list their homes for free, upload photos, set a price, and reach millions of buyers. As an investor, you can filter specifically for 'For Sale By Owner' listings in any zip code or city. Zillow also shows how long a listing has been active — a property sitting for 30+ days is often a sign the seller is getting frustrated and may be more open to a below-market offer. Start here for sheer volume.
2. Craigslist — Raw, Unfiltered FSBO Leads

Craigslist is old-school, but it still works. Many sellers — particularly older homeowners or those in rural and suburban markets — post their properties here with no photos, minimal description, and a phone number. That's actually an opportunity. These sellers haven't invested in marketing, which means they're often price-flexible. Search under 'Real Estate For Sale' in your target city and filter for owner listings. Set up a saved search and check it daily. The deals here are rough around the edges, but that's where margin lives.
3. Facebook Marketplace — A Growing FSBO Goldmine

Facebook Marketplace has quietly become one of the best places to find FSBO homes, especially in mid-sized markets. Sellers post quickly, often without much thought about pricing strategy, and the direct messaging feature makes outreach easy. You can also join local Facebook real estate groups where homeowners post properties before they ever hit any official platform. Search terms like 'house for sale by owner [city]' or 'FSBO [zip code]' inside Facebook groups and Marketplace to surface opportunities competitors are missing.
4. FSBO.com — Dedicated FSBO Platform

FSBO.com is a site built entirely around for sale by owner listings. Sellers pay a small flat fee to list, which means every property here has an owner who is serious enough to put money into marketing — but still committed to avoiding agent commissions. The site lets you search by state, city, or zip code and filter by price range, property type, and square footage. Because it's less trafficked than Zillow, you'll face less competition from other buyers when you reach out.
5. ForSaleByOwner.com — Another Niche FSBO Directory

ForSaleByOwner.com is similar to FSBO.com in structure but has its own unique set of listings. Some sellers post on one and not the other, so it's worth checking both. The site also gives sellers the option to upgrade to MLS syndication, but even the base listings are visible to the public. Look for listings with limited photos or sparse descriptions — these sellers often need help and are open to investor conversations.
6. LoopNet and Auction.com — For Investors Targeting Multi-Family and Distressed

If you're focused on multi-family FSBO properties or distressed assets, LoopNet has a commercial FSBO section worth monitoring. Auction.com, while technically an auction platform, surfaces many FSBO-adjacent listings from motivated sellers who want to move fast. These platforms cater to a more sophisticated seller, but the deal sizes are often larger and the negotiation dynamics favor buyers who come prepared.

Pro Tip: Don't just browse FSBO sites passively. Set up email alerts on Zillow and Craigslist for new FSBO listings in your target zip codes. Speed matters — being the first investor to call a new FSBO listing dramatically increases your chances of getting a deal. Aim to contact new listings within 24 hours of posting.
How to Approach FSBO Sellers as an Investor

Finding the listing is only step one. FSBO sellers chose not to use an agent, which sometimes means they're skeptical of professionals. Your approach needs to feel collaborative, not predatory. Lead with questions: Why are you selling? What's your timeline? Have you had other offers? Listen more than you talk. FSBO sellers who've been sitting on the market for 45–60 days are especially receptive because their frustration is real and their motivation has grown.

items: Call within 24 hours of a new listing going live — early contact builds rapport before competitors arrive
Ask open-ended questions to understand the seller's timeline, motivation, and flexibility on price
Offer a free, no-obligation cash offer rather than leading with a lowball number
Mention the speed and simplicity of an investor sale versus the uncertainty of retail buyers with financing contingencies
Follow up consistently — most FSBO deals close after the 3rd or 4th contact, not the first

sections.content: The best deal you'll ever do is the one your competition gave up on. Most investors quit after one follow-up call. The money is in the follow-up. — Common wisdom among top wholesalers
Combine FSBO Leads With Other Off-Market Strategies

FSBO websites are powerful, but the most successful investors layer multiple lead sources. FSBO sellers who listed publicly are just one slice of the motivated seller universe. You should also be building lists from probate court records — check out our guide on [Probate Real Estate Leads: How to Find and Approach](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/probate-real-estate-leads) — and using tools to identify [absentee owner lists](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/absentee-owner-list-deals) who may be ready to sell but haven't listed publicly yet. For physical scouting, [driving for dollars apps](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/best-driving-for-dollars-apps) can surface distressed properties before they ever hit any website.

When you find a FSBO deal that looks promising, the next step is running the numbers fast. Use our free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to estimate your maximum allowable offer based on the ARV, repair costs, and your target profit margin. Knowing your numbers before you call a seller puts you in a position of confidence — and that confidence closes deals.
Quick Step-by-Step: From FSBO Listing to Offer

items: Step 1: Set up daily alerts on Zillow, Craigslist, and FSBO.com for your target markets
Step 2: When a new listing appears, research the property address via county records and Google Maps
Step 3: Run a quick ARV estimate using comparable sales in the area
Step 4: Calculate your max offer using the 70% rule (or your preferred formula) with our free Deal Calculator
Step 5: Call the seller within 24 hours, ask questions, and build rapport before presenting any number
Step 6: Follow up every 5–7 days until they accept, list with an agent, or sell elsewhere
Step 7: Once under contract, assign or close based on your exit strategy
